passage:
"Knock knock!"
"Who's there?" said her grandmother Indu.
"Banana!"
"Banana who?"
"Banana... purple!" Payal, five, giggled so hard she slid off the sofa.
"Why is that funny?"
"Because purple!"
"Say it again in a silly voice."
"Zibbly zobbly purple!" Payal rolled on the rug, and Indu laughed until she had to wipe her eyes.

qa.q: What did Payal answer to "Banana who?"
What does Payal feel about her own joke, and how can you tell?
qa.a: She is delighted and finds it hilarious, shown by giggling so hard she slid off the sofa. She may not yet know why it is funny.

qa.q: How could Indu keep the play going?
qa.a: Laugh, and play along with silly words and rhymes instead of correcting the punchline.

qa.q: How might Indu see Payal's joke?
qa.a: As delightful, even though the punchline does not quite work. 😊

grounding: Shows a preschooler telling a knock-knock joke that misses the punchline and giggling at nonsense words.

passage: Note from Eshaan, nursery teacher. At circle time Mridul (5) told a joke. "Why did the chicken sit on the clock? Because... it was hungry!" He laughed loudly and the others laughed with him, though I doubt anyone knew why. Later he chanted "wibble-wobble-woo" to the rain rhyme. I said it back and he clapped. Tomorrow: a nonsense-rhyme corner. 🙂

qa.q: What did Mridul say the chicken was?
What might Mridul be feeling as he tells the joke?
qa.a: Playful and pleased at making others laugh. He may not yet grasp why jokes are funny.

qa.q: What did Eshaan do in response?
qa.a: Eshaan repeated the nonsense words back and planned a nonsense-rhyme corner.

qa.q: How might the other children see Mridul's joke?
qa.a: They laughed along because laughter is catching, not necessarily because they understood it.

grounding: Shows a preschooler telling a joke that misses the point and chanting nonsense words for the fun of the pattern.
